newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus 1997 budget deficit rises, no new taxes.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus 1997 budget deficit rises, no new taxes.

text.p: Cyprus's cabinet on Thursday approved the 1997 state budget raising the deficit by almost 14 percent over projected figures for 1996 and without provisions for tax increases in the coming year.
Net spending is forecast at 1.48 billion pounds ($3.20 billion) against revenue of 1.09 billion, giving a deficit of 388.8 million pounds.
Projected spending for the 1996 year is 1.35 billion pounds, against revenue of 1.01 billion, yielding a deficit of 341.7 million pounds.
Finance Minister Christodoulos Christodoulou said the fiscal deficit is expected to be 2.9 percent of gross domestic product in 1996 compared with an original estimate of 4.1 percent.
Preliminary calculations for 1997 show a four percent fiscal deficit, but Christodoulou said it could finally fall to three percent because it is normal not to spend all budgeted resources.
"The budgets we are tabling are governed by a spirit of frugality and fiscal discipline," he told journalists after the cabinet meeting.

Christodoulou said the budget, to be presented on September 19 for approval by the House of Representatives, did not include any provision for 1997 tax increases, but he would not commit himself to saying that tax hikes are excluded entirely.
"In 1996 there will be no increase of any tax and that includes value added tax, (VAT) " he said. VAT is now eight percent.
He added that indices showed Cyprus meeting the economic criteria set by the Maastricht treaty for European Union countries. Cyprus will start accession talks with the EU in late 1997 or early 1998.
Public debt, excluding intergovernmental, is expected to fluctuate at around 52.5 percent of GDP in 1997, compared to a projected figure of 54 percent of GDP for 1996.
Inflation is not expected to exceed three percent, Christodoulou said. ($=0.46 pounds)
